Figure 1:Single- and multi-input multi-turn editing.TailSteer substantially reduces cumulative drift over editing
turns while retaining the base model’s (FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B) editing capability.

Figure 2:Trajectory tail remains correctable.Low-frequency content is recovered early, whereas
higher-frequency details are primarily recovered near the tail (top),
while preservation error in unchanged regions continues to decrease but remains non-zero at the endpoint (bottom).

Figure 3:Data curation of preservation-aware trajectory endpoints.We construct supervision from rollouts of the frozen base editor using two
complementary edit types: (a) identity editing provides full-image preservation
trajectories, while (b) local editing provides partial-preservation trajectories
with spatially localized changes. Only samples that pass the corresponding
sanity checks are retained and cached as training trajectories for subsequent
TailSteer optimization.

Figure 4:One-step terminal intervention: benefits and limitations.(a) We fine-tune FLUX.2-klein-9B with supervision only at the final sampling
step, steering from the cached pre-terminal statexτbasex_{\tau}^{\mathrm{base}}toward the preservation-aware targetx1tgtx_{1}^{\mathrm{tgt}}.
(b) The base model accumulates visible identity drift over repeated edits (top row). Applying the fine-tuned model only at the final step markedly improves long-horizon preservation (middle row), whereas using it throughout sampling causes desaturation and detail loss (bottom row). Therefore, it is necessary to preserve the earlier dynamics.

Figure 5:On-policy training of TailSteer.At randomly sampled training statesxk1x_{k_{1}}andxk2x_{k_{2}}, the refined
model receives region-dependent supervision. In the prior region, its
prediction is matched to the frozen base model’s velocityvbasev^{\mathrm{base}}; in the transition region, the targetv∗v^{*}progressively
blendsvbasev^{\mathrm{base}}with the preservation velocityvpresv^{\mathrm{pres}}towardx1tgtx_{1}^{\mathrm{tgt}}.
To obtain these states on-policy, the refined model rolls out from the nearest
preceding cached anchor in prior region, and from the fixed steering-onset
state in transition region. The velocity target is then recomputed at the
state actually reached by the refined model, with gradients applied only to
its prediction at the sampled step.

Figure 6:20-turn qualitative comparison.While competing methods exhibit cumulative visual drift, TailSteer faithfully preserves the original tabletop color and previously established details, including the coffee cup, latte art, and cookie on the right, even after 20 successive editing turns.

Figure 7:Multi-input multi-turn editing.TailSteer retains base models’ multi-image editing capabilities while substantially reducing cumulative drift, preserving backgrounds during multi-person and multi-object compositing and the girl’s dress details across successive skeleton-guided edits.

Figure 9:Qualitative comparison after 10 editing turns.TailSteer substantially reduces background drift while retaining the requested object edits across different backbones. For Klein, bypassing inter-turn VAE conversions further preserves the original background colors and details.
Figure 10:Ablation of training strategies.With the same training data, full TailSteer better balances preserving the base model’s editing capabilities with enhancing multi-turn drift resistance.
